title: The Baker and The Soldier
author: William Saville
content:
The city was quiet compared to the front. Far from the thunder of shells, its streets hummed with the gentler noise of daily survival: the rattle of empty carts, the hollow bark of dogs, and the thin laughter of children who had learned too young what hunger was. In this muted corner of the war, people still pretended at normalcy, though the absence of plenty clung to the air like soot. It was here that a soldier, broken in both body and spirit, slipped into shadow. His uniform hung loose on him, stiff with dried blood, and his boots were worn nearly through. He had gone AWOL, not out of cowardice, but because the pain had become unbearable, and because the voice inside his head whispered that to keep marching forward was simply to march into death.

For days he wandered, delirious, without food or water. His tongue was a dry stone in his mouth, his skin burning with fever. He carried the look of a man already claimed by the grave, his eyes glassy with thirst, his body trembling with each ragged step. He stumbled into fields and then into the fringes of farmland, his breath shallow, his mind swimming with fragments of memory, laughter with comrades, the sting of shrapnel, the sound of rain striking tin roofs in a village far behind him. By the time he found the barn, he could no longer distinguish dream from reality. The soldier collapsed across the straw, his body surrendering. Darkness took him swiftly.

The barn belonged to a baker. Once, he had been famous in the city for his pastries, layered confections that melted on the tongue, chocolates that shone like jewels, and cakes so decadent they made children gasp. But in wartime, sugar was a dream and flour was rationed away to the front. Still, the baker persisted, not for wealth, but for the people. From his cellar, still half-full with what little he had saved, he made bread and meat pies, giving most of it freely to the poor who passed his door. He himself lived on scraps. He hated the war, despised the way it starved his neighbors, yet he did not curse the soldiers. He knew better. They were men caught in a machine larger than themselves.

That evening, carrying in a basket of loaves, the baker noticed something wrong. A door to the barn, usually shut tight against the wind, stood ajar. He frowned, setting his basket aside, and stepped inside. The smell of hay and dust filled his lungs, but beneath it lay another scent: sweat, blood, sickness. His eyes fell on the soldier, a body crumpled in straw, chest rising shallowly, lips cracked and colorless. The man looked half-dead already. For a long moment the baker simply stood, his breath caught between caution and pity. A deserter, he thought. A hunted man. Yet in the soldier’s brokenness there was no malice, only suffering.

Kneeling slowly, the baker touched the man’s forehead and felt the heat of fever burning through skin stretched thin. The soldier stirred, but did not wake. The baker sighed, a sound heavy with resignation and compassion. He could have turned him in. He could have shut the door and left him to fate. But instead, he rose, fetched water, and returned to kneel once more. “You poor soul,” he whispered, voice low in the dim barn. “You won’t die here, not like this.” And in that quiet promise, the first thread of something fragile and lasting was spun between them.

Arras was not untouched, though it tried to be. The cathedral stood in ruin, its bones reaching upward against the sky, while the marketplace whispered of what it once had been. Families rationed what little they had, the city’s laughter muted, its beauty scarred. Yet compared to the mud-sunk trenches just days away, Arras was a sanctuary, a fragile heartbeat in the shadow of war. Into this city, into a baker’s barn, the soldier had stumbled, carrying the front lines within his broken body.

For two days he drifted between worlds. Fever burned him, shaking his limbs and twisting his breath into broken sobs. Sometimes he cried out, reaching for a rifle no longer in his hands, or for brothers already buried beneath foreign earth. The baker watched, quiet and steady, a sentinel beside the straw. He had drawn water from the well, soaked cloths in its coolness, and pressed them against the soldier’s brow. At times he spooned thin broth past the soldier’s cracked lips, whispering, “Easy now, you’re safe here, hush.”

At night the soldier’s nightmares clawed through the barn’s walls. He gasped as if drowning, eyes wide at shadows only he could see. The baker would startle from his sleep on the floor nearby, rise, and take the soldier’s trembling hands in his own flour-roughened palms. He would sit through the terror until the soldier’s breath steadied, until the sweat on his skin cooled. He spoke little, for words rarely mattered, but his presence was solid, a quiet stone in the flood.

On the third evening, the baker carried a bucket of warm water into the barn. The soldier, weak but awake, stirred at the sound. His face was gaunt, beard ragged, his eyes dulled by fever but still alive. Without asking, the baker set the bucket down, wet a cloth, and began to wash the grime from the man’s neck and arms. The soldier flinched, as if unused to gentleness, but he did not pull away. “Rest,” the baker murmured, dipping the cloth again. “No one will find you here.” He did not ask the man’s name, some things could wait.

Outside, the city sighed under rations and quiet hunger, women queuing for bread that barely filled their children’s bellies, soldiers on leave passing through with haunted eyes. Yet inside the barn, time bent itself around two figures: one broken by war, the other hardened by survival yet softened by pity. In the simple acts of feeding, washing, and soothing, a fragile kinship grew, born not of words but of need, of one man’s refusal to let another die unseen.

By the fourth morning, the fever broke. The soldier’s eyes, once glazed, now flickered with awareness, though his body remained weak as clay. The baker was kneeling with a bowl of broth when the soldier rasped his first clear words, no longer fevered fragments, but a voice stitched together by will. The baker paused, then smiled gently, as if they had been waiting for this moment together.

“My name is Lucien,” he said at last, his voice low, almost careful. He set the bowl aside, folded his rough hands over his knees, and waited.

The soldier’s gaze wavered, cautious. His lips parted, and he hesitated long enough that the silence became heavy. Then, with a breath drawn sharp as glass, he whispered, “Étienne.” His eyes darted away, as if the falsehood might reveal itself in his face. But Lucien did not press. He simply nodded, repeating the name softly, accepting the lie as though it were truth.

When strength returned enough for walking, Lucien offered more than bread and broth. He offered questions. “What will you do now?” he asked one evening, while they sat at the heavy table inside the quiet house. The soldier, Étienne, stared into the fire. “I don’t know,” he confessed. “I only knew I couldn’t go back. My family expected me to march forever, to die if I must. My grandfather wore the uniform. My father too. The firstborn son doesn’t choose, he serves. And so I did. Until I couldn’t.” His hands trembled faintly as he spoke, as if memory still rattled in his bones.

Lucien listened, then shared in return. He told of his own life: how plague had stolen his parents before he could remember their faces, how priests had raised him in cold halls until the day they declared him a man at sixteen and sent him into the world. He spoke of the baker who took him as apprentice, who left him the house and the ovens when he died. “I never married,” Lucien said simply, his eyes on the hearth’s glow. “Work was enough. And perhaps I knew I had no place in that kind of life.” He shrugged, not unkindly.

Neither of them could say their birthdays with certainty, records had burned in churches or gone missing in war. They carried only guesses. Lucien thought himself to be twenty-seven, perhaps twenty-eight. Étienne claimed twenty-one or twenty-two, though even that was spoken like a guess. They shared their fragments without shame, as though the gaps themselves were another bond.

In time, the soldier moved into the spare room of the house adjoining the bakery. No words were exchanged about it, Lucien simply left the door open, and Étienne carried his few belongings inside. Soon after, he began helping around the house: hauling water, chopping wood, scrubbing dishes. Lucien protested gently, “You don’t owe me anything.” But Étienne shook his head, his voice firm despite the softness in his eyes. “I won’t sit idle while you carry me. Let me earn my place here.” And so it was: a soldier turned runaway, and a baker who fed the poor, learning the rhythm of a shared life neither had expected.

Winter bled into spring, and spring into summer. The days blurred into a rhythm neither man had expected to find. Lucien rose early each morning to fire the ovens, Étienne trailing behind soon after to haul sacks of flour or fetch water. By mid-morning, the scent of bread filled the air, and a line of townsfolk gathered at the door, waiting for loaves and meat pies that Lucien gave freely. Étienne, once hesitant to be seen, now handed out parcels with quiet hands, his soldier’s posture softened into something almost humble. The poor learned his face but asked no questions, and Lucien noticed how often their eyes lingered not on suspicion, but gratitude.

In the evenings, when the work was done and the streets were hushed, they read together. Lucien kept a few worn volumes, poems, prayer-books, and stories left behind by the priest who had once taught him his letters. Étienne read aloud haltingly at first, his voice rough from disuse, but Lucien never mocked, only encouraged. Some nights they fell asleep mid-page on the faded couch, heads tipping toward one another, arms brushing until sleep made them still.

The days were stitched with smaller moments, unspoken and fragile. Étienne’s hand brushing Lucien’s as they carried a pot between them. Lucien’s sleeve ghosting across Étienne’s arm as they reached for the same loaf. Neither spoke of it, but both felt the pauses, those silences that trembled with something unsaid. Once, while Étienne stirred broth at the stove, Lucien’s hand reached past him for the ladle, and the brief press of chest to shoulder lingered longer than it should have. Both men drew back quickly, but not before the air between them changed, charged with quiet electricity.

The townsfolk noticed their closeness, though not with malice. Children laughed as Étienne lifted them high when they came to collect bread, widows left the bakery with a blessing whispered under their breath. The two men were spoken of simply as housemates, a soldier convalescing and a baker who took him in. Yet the town’s silence was deliberate, a tacit agreement that some truths need not be named aloud.

By summer, their days were woven tightly together. Étienne helped knead dough until his arms ached, Lucien teaching him the patient art of bread rising, the warmth of yeast alive under cloth. On hot evenings they sat outside, listening to the faint hum of crickets, trading stories, one about a boyhood on priests’ bread and discipline, the other about a youth gilded with duty and expectation. And in all those months, in every touch and every pause, something unspoken deepened, like dough left to rise in quiet warmth, biding its time.

When Lucien announced he must travel, Étienne’s chest tightened though he hid it beneath a soldier’s stillness. There were families several towns over who were starving, children faint with hunger, and Lucien had promised aid. Étienne offered to go too, but Lucien shook his head. “No. The soldiers on the roads… they might recognize you. Stay. Keep the house warm.” The soldier nodded, though inside, fear twisted. He watched Lucien leave at dawn with a cart of bread, shoulders squared against the horizon. The road swallowed him, and the house felt emptier than Étienne had imagined possible.

Days passed. Then weeks. Each evening, Étienne sat by the window, waiting for footsteps that never came. He tried to keep busy, hauling wood, sweeping, mending, but the quiet gnawed at him. At night, sleep brought no peace. The war returned in dreams: mud in his mouth, comrades’ cries, the thunder of shells. But worse still was the waking silence, the absence of Lucien’s voice. He could not name the ache inside him, could only pace the rooms until finally, one night, he reached for the bottle hidden at the back of the cupboard.

The wine burned his throat, dulled his thoughts, and then, cruelly, sharpened them. He stared at the firelight trembling against the walls and felt the weight of what he had been denying. He was in love, with Lucien’s steady hands, his quiet smile, his presence that anchored him when terror clawed at his chest. But it was wrong, wasn’t it? Two men, bound in ways the world would not forgive. He tried to laugh it off, but the laugh cracked and broke, and soon the bottle was his only companion as his defenses fell like crumbling walls.

On the fifteenth night, the door creaked open. Étienne jolted upright, the bottle slipping from his hand. Lucien stood framed in the doorway, shoulders bowed beneath exhaustion. His face was gray with travel, his clothes dusted with grief. He had seen death again, the kind that made Arras seem like a miracle of peace. Yet when his eyes fell on Étienne, the weight seemed to lift, if only slightly. “You’re here,” Lucien murmured, a weary smile ghosting his lips.

Étienne rose unsteadily, his heart a storm. He crossed the space between them, his hand trembling as it found Lucien’s cheek. The warmth of skin against his palm shattered the last of his restraint. “My name isn’t Étienne,” he whispered, his voice thick with wine and truth. “It’s Julien.” For a moment, the world held its breath. Then he leaned forward, desperate and certain all at once, and kissed him deeply, every fear, every forbidden longing pouring into the space between their mouths.

Lucien stiffened as Julien’s lips met his, instinct tugging him back toward caution. For half a breath, he tried to retreat, hands hovering as though to push away. But Julien’s grip held firm, his palm warm against Lucien’s cheek, his mouth pressing with a need that trembled on the edge of desperation. “Don’t,” Julien whispered against his lips, voice breaking. “Not now.” His other hand fisted in Lucien’s shirt and drew him closer.

And Lucien, tired, heartsore, starved of touch, let go. The wall he had built, brick by brick, crumbled in the space of a heartbeat. He surged forward, weaving his hand into Julien’s hair, pulling him nearer until their breaths mingled, until the kiss deepened and became something dangerous, intoxicating. His body shivered with the newness of it. He had never kissed anyone before, never even allowed himself to want. Now he wanted nothing but this, Julien’s lips, Julien’s warmth, the feeling of being desired.

For Julien, the taste was unfamiliar but not unknown. He had kissed before, yes, but always as duty, as performance, as the golden son keeping up appearances. His past embraces had been hollow, bodies pressed together while his mind reached elsewhere, to glimpses of strangers, fleeting sparks of forbidden imaginings. Never had he been present in the moment, never had he been filled rather than emptied by a kiss. Until now. Lucien’s mouth was different, unpracticed, clumsy even, but real. Real enough to unravel him.

The loneliness they both carried fell away in that embrace, like armor cast aside after battle. Julien pressed harder, gasping softly into Lucien’s mouth, and Lucien answered with a low sound that was half-surprise, half-need. Their fears, the wrongness of two men, the weight of war, the hunger of empty years, faded beneath the fierce rightness of lips against lips, of hands holding tight as if they’d both drown without the other.

When at last they parted, it was only to breathe, foreheads pressed together, their chests heaving in unison. Julien’s eyes were wet, Lucien’s wide with awe. Silence stretched, heavy and fragile, but neither man let go. It was as though they feared if they broke the contact, the spell would vanish, and they would wake to find it was nothing more than a dream.

Lucien’s breath trembled against Julien’s cheek. His lips were still tingling, his heart hammering so hard it frightened him. He pulled back a fraction, searching Julien’s eyes as though for permission to speak, to exist in this new, impossible truth. “That was…” His voice faltered, softer than a prayer. “That was my first.”

Julien froze, guilt and wonder colliding in his chest. He cupped Lucien’s face in both hands, his thumbs brushing along his jaw. “Your first kiss?”

Lucien nodded once, eyes shining, vulnerable as an open wound. Julien’s chest ached at the sight. He wanted to apologize, to say he shouldn’t have stolen it like this, drunk and desperate. But Lucien’s hand still threaded in his hair, holding him there. And when Lucien tugged, just slightly, Julien understood.

Their mouths found each other again, slower this time, almost reverent. Lucien sighed into it, tasting the unfamiliar, letting himself drown in the warmth. He had never known desire like this, never imagined it could live inside him. He broke away only long enough to whisper, “I thought I wasn’t made for this. For wanting. But with you…” His voice cracked, and he silenced himself with another kiss.

Julien groaned softly, pressing his forehead to Lucien’s, their breaths mingling. “You don’t know,” he murmured, words spilling out in ragged confession. “Every time I kissed someone else before, I was somewhere else in my head. I imagined faces, strangers, men I wasn’t allowed to look at too long. I was never there, never whole. But now… now I don’t have to pretend.” His fingers slid to the back of Lucien’s neck, pulling him close, grounding himself in the reality of this impossible moment.

Lucien shuddered, his own hand sliding down Julien’s arm, clutching at his sleeve as though he might vanish if he let go. “It feels wrong,” he whispered, “the world would call it wrong. But I’ve never felt anything so right.”

Julien swallowed, kissed him again, softer, almost pleading. “Then let the world be wrong.”

And in the quiet house, with only the firelight trembling on the walls, their loneliness collapsed between them, replaced with something raw and real. They kissed until the need for words faded, until silence carried its own language, fingers entwined, lips brushing, hearts steadying in a rhythm both terrifying and true.

Their breaths slowed, the urgency of the kiss ebbing into something gentler. Neither wished to let go, but both knew the night could not be all fire. Slowly, as if afraid of breaking the fragile peace they’d stumbled into, Lucien guided Julien toward the couch. They sat side by side, shoulders pressed together, the silence stretching warm instead of heavy.

The book they had left on the table weeks ago still waited, pages marked by a folded scrap of paper. Lucien picked it up with a small, almost shy smile. “Read to me,” he said, voice roughened but steady. Julien took the book, though his eyes lingered on Lucien longer than the page. He began to read, words halting at first, then smoothing into rhythm, while Lucien leaned against him, his head resting on Julien’s shoulder.

Every few lines, the words faltered because their mouths found each other again. Brief, stolen kisses, softer now, unhurried, as though they were testing the shape of this new closeness. Each kiss was a punctuation, each touch a quiet declaration. The story in the book wove on, but their own story threaded itself in the spaces between the words.

The fire dimmed as the night deepened. Lucien’s arm wrapped around Julien, and Julien tucked closer into the warmth, his hand brushing against Lucien’s chest in a way that felt protective, not possessive. The book slipped from Julien’s grasp at last, tumbling to the floor with a soft thud. Neither stirred to pick it up.

They drifted into sleep together on the worn couch, bodies folded into one another, the last glow of the embers painting them in fading orange light. Outside, the city lay in silence, carrying its quiet sorrows. Inside, for the first time in years, neither man slept alone.

The morning after, sunlight slipped pale through the shutters. Julien stirred first, confused by the weight pressed against him. Then memory rushed back, the kisses, the closeness, the book fallen to the floor. His breath caught, but before panic could rise, Lucien shifted in his sleep, his face softened in a peace Julien had never seen there before. For a fleeting moment, Julien let himself look, really look, and feel the ache of wanting.

When Lucien woke, their eyes met. Neither spoke of the night, but neither pulled away until at last Lucien cleared his throat, rising carefully. “We should… start the ovens,” he murmured, as though routine could steady trembling hearts. Julien nodded, though the warmth where Lucien had been lingered on his skin.

Days fell back into their rhythm. Bread was baked, the poor were fed, neighbors were greeted with nods and smiles. To the town, nothing had changed. But behind closed doors, in moments stolen between duties, everything had shifted. A hand brushing too long against another, a kiss stolen in the shadow of the pantry, lips pressing together quickly before a knock at the bakery door scattered them apart. At night, they retreated to their separate rooms, shutting their doors as if to contain what had been unleashed.

Yet silence carried its own weight. Lying in their beds, both men stared at ceilings, listening to the faint movements of the other, each aching with the same thought: one step more, and everything would change forever. Fear held them apart, even as longing drew them closer.

One evening, after another long day of feeding weary faces, they returned home exhausted. Lucien moved toward his room as always, Julien trailing with a faint smile meant to hide disappointment. But when Lucien reached his doorway, he paused. Slowly, deliberately, he left the door open behind him. He glanced back once, meeting Julien’s eyes, no words spoken. The invitation was quiet, but undeniable.

Julien stood frozen in the hall, his breath shallow, his heart a drumbeat. Every warning screamed at him to turn away, to retreat to safety. But the soft light spilling through the open door beckoned, and Lucien’s eyes held him fast.

Months passed, and their relationship bloomed and blossomed among the decay of their town. Some townsfolk suspected, but they said not a word, as they had never seen their baker so happy, and they knew that they relied on him for survival, but also realized that love could take many forms. Many townsfolk who suspected were disgusted, but mostly kept their disgust to themselves,but occasionally Lucien and Julien would find nasty notes in the mailbox telling them that what they were doing was a sin. But Julien and Lucien ignored them. They felt that they finally found peace and acceptance together, and nothing could change that.

One day, Arras was entered by the allies, seeking rooms to stay in, food for their bellies, and the war had finally arrived in their town. But there was a problem, out of the many troops that had entered, one was Julien’s, and there was a huge risk of him being caught, and arrested for desertion.

That evening, the air carried a metallic tang of incoming soldiers, the clatter of boots against cobblestones louder than the town had known for months. Julien’s chest tightened as he watched men in uniform march past the bakery, rifles slung, eyes wary. He had hoped, foolishly, that he could remain invisible, that the quiet life he and Lucien had carved out might shield him from the world he had fled. But fate, as it often did, had other plans.

Lucien returned from the ovens, wiping flour from his hands, and saw the rigid set of Julien’s shoulders. “Julien?” he asked softly, following his gaze toward the street. Julien’s jaw tightened, he could not speak.

Soldiers paused outside the bakery, scanning faces. One of them, a man whose uniform marked him as the officer in charge, looked closer at Julien, whose gait and face were unmistakable. Fear coiled in Julien’s stomach. He wanted to flee, to run into the fields, to hide in the haystack where he had once nearly died. But the soldiers were faster, methodical.

“Julien… is that you?” the officer called, stepping toward him. His eyes were sharp, and Julien knew that recognition had come too late.

Lucien moved to block him, his voice trembling. “He’s not a threat. He’s, he’s helping me. Please…”

The officer’s expression hardened. “You are a deserter. You know what must happen.”

Julien’s knees buckled beneath him. He turned to Lucien, eyes wide and terrified. “Run… you have to get out of here.”

“No,” Lucien whispered, grabbing his hand. “We stay together.”

The officer raised his pistol. Julien’s chest tightened, the world narrowing to the room, to Lucien, to the warmth that had kept him alive. For a heartbeat, it seemed impossible. They could not die here. Not like this.

The shot rang.

Lucien fell first, blood blooming across his shirt, eyes wide with disbelief. Julien screamed, reaching for him, but the officer struck Julien’s shoulder with the rifle butt, sending him to the floor. Julien could barely breathe, the warmth of Lucien slipping away, the life he had fought to protect extinguished before his eyes.

They dragged Julien outside, the town silent save for the distant cries of children, the soft whine of the wind across broken rooftops. Lucien lay crumpled in the doorway of the bakery, his hand stretched toward Julien’s, a silent plea frozen in the dying light. Julien tried to speak, tried to call his name, but the words caught in his throat.

As the soldiers marched him away in handcuffs, Julien’s eyes never left Lucien. The baker’s face, peaceful and pale, haunted him even as the world swallowed him whole. He would carry that memory, the smell of fresh bread, the warmth of stolen kisses, the quiet heartbeat of a life almost lived, through the rest of his days, a ghost of love in a world built on ruin.

Arras, for all its fragile hope and hidden happiness, had given them a brief, shining respite. But in the end, war had claimed its toll. Julien walked away, a deserter still, but now carrying a grief that no bread, no kindness, no stolen love could ever fill.

And the bakery stood silent, ovens cold, a monument to what had been: two hearts entwined for a fleeting moment, extinguished by the world outside their fragile walls.
